lessons.title: How Your Employer Calculates TDS on Salary Every Month

body.text: Your employer does not work out TDS one month at a time. It estimates your tax for the whole year, spreads it across the months left, and recalculates every time something changes.

children.text: Aditi joined a Gurugram fintech firm in April 2026 on a salary of ₹20,00,000 a year. Her April payslip showed ₹16,033 deducted as income tax. In October, after a ₹2,00,000 performance bonus, the deduction jumped to ₹24,050 and stayed there until March. She assumed payroll had made a mistake. It had not. This lesson shows exactly how those numbers were produced, so you can check your own payslip line by line.
The Rule: Tax at Your Average Rate

markDefs.definition: Your estimated total income tax for the year divided by your estimated taxable income. Salary TDS is spread across the year using this rate, rather than applying the top slab rate to each month.

children.text: Under Section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (formerly Section 192), your employer must deduct tax on salary at the
average rate of tax
on your estimated income for the whole tax year. In practice, payroll software follows a simple loop every month.

body.latex: \text{Monthly TDS} = \dfrac{\text{Estimated tax for the year} - \text{TDS already deducted this year}}{\text{Months of salary remaining, including this one}}
body.caption: Recalculated each month, so any change in salary, bonus or declarations flows into the remaining months

cells: Adds up salary already paid and salary expected for the rest of the year
Standard deduction under Section 19 (formerly 16): ₹75,000 in the new regime, ₹50,000 in the old. Old regime also allows exemptions like HRA
Declared investments and payments such as Section 123 (formerly 80C) and Section 126 (formerly 80D)
Not available in the new regime
4. Apply slab rates, rebate and cess
Tax on taxable income, less any rebate under Section 156 (formerly 87A), plus 4% health and education cess
Divides what is still due by the months remaining

children.text: The slab rates payroll uses for tax year 2026-27

Budget 2026 left personal income tax slabs unchanged, so the rates introduced for 2025-26 continue. The new regime, under Section 202 (formerly Section 115BAC), is the default. The old regime applies only if you tell your employer you want it.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Last Step
body.textWithBlank: After slab tax and any rebate, payroll adds health and education cess at ___% before spreading the tax across the year.
body.explanation: Cess is 4% of income tax (plus surcharge, if any). For Aditi that is 4% of ₹1,85,000 = ₹7,400, taking her annual tax to ₹1,92,400.

children.text: When Something Changes Mid-Year

Because the estimate is rebuilt every month, a change in October affects only October to March. When Aditi's ₹2,00,000 bonus was confirmed, her projected gross salary rose to ₹22,00,000 and her estimated tax for the year to ₹2,40,500. By then ₹96,200 had already been deducted over six months.

body.caption: The extra tax on the bonus is spread over the six remaining months

body.title: Aditi's monthly salary TDS, tax year 2026-27

children.text: Not every payroll team spreads it this way. Some deduct the entire extra tax on a bonus in the month it is paid, which produces one very large deduction instead of six moderate ones. Both methods end the year at the same total. What matters is that by March, TDS matches the estimated tax.

body.title: Quick Check: Why Did TDS Jump?
body.question: Aditi's TDS rose from ₹16,033 to ₹24,050 a month after her bonus. Which statement is correct?
options: Her bonus is taxed at a special higher rate for one-time payments
Her total estimated tax rose, and the extra tax is being recovered from fewer remaining months
Payroll is deducting advance tax on her behalf
Her regime was switched to the old regime automatically
body.explanation: A bonus is ordinary salary taxed at slab rates. It pushed part of her income into the 25% slab and raised her yearly tax by ₹48,100. Because six months had already passed at the old rate, the shortfall had to be recovered over the remaining six, so each of those months carries more than its share.

children.text: The ₹12 Lakh Rebate and Marginal Relief

In the new regime, a rebate under Section 156 (formerly 87A) wipes out tax completely when taxable income is ₹12,00,000 or less. Add the ₹75,000 standard deduction and a salary of up to ₹12,75,000 attracts no tax, so payroll deducts no TDS at all.

body.title: Try It: Rebate Territory
body.prompt: Ravi, a bank clerk in Bhopal, earns a salary of ₹12,75,000 in tax year 2026-27, stays in the new regime and has no other income. How much TDS should his employer deduct each month?
body.explanation: Taxable income is ₹12,75,000 minus ₹75,000 = ₹12,00,000. Slab tax is ₹60,000, and the Section 156 rebate of up to ₹60,000 cancels it entirely. With no tax due for the year, there is nothing to deduct.

body.title: Earning just above ₹12,75,000? How marginal relief protects you

children.text: Without extra protection, crossing ₹12,00,000 of taxable income by one rupee would lose the whole rebate and create a tax bill of about ₹60,000. Marginal relief prevents that: your tax cannot exceed the amount by which your taxable income crosses ₹12,00,000.

Priya, a school administrator in Mysuru, earns ₹13,00,000. Taxable income is ₹12,25,000. Normal slab tax would be ₹63,750, but her income is only ₹25,000 above ₹12,00,000, so her tax is capped at ₹25,000. Cess is added on the capped figure.
Old Regime: Same Loop, Different Inputs

The monthly loop is identical in the old regime. What changes is step 3: payroll subtracts the deductions you declare and prove, using Form 124 (formerly Form 12BB). Take Karan, a consultant in Pune on the same ₹20,00,000 salary as Aditi, who opted for the old regime and declared ₹1,50,000 under Section 123 (formerly 80C) and ₹25,000 of health insurance under Section 126 (formerly 80D).

With only ₹1,75,000 of deductions, the old regime costs Karan ₹1,66,400 more for the year. The old regime only wins when exemptions such as HRA and home loan interest are large. Lesson 2 shows how declarations change the picture.

body.text: If you do not tell your employer which regime you want, payroll must use the new regime. You generally make this choice once at the start of the year and cannot keep switching it with payroll month to month. If you have no business income, you can still pick the other regime when filing your return, and any difference is settled as a refund or extra tax.

children.text: Other Income You Can Tell Payroll About

Payroll only knows about your salary unless you tell it more. Section 392 lets you share details of certain other income and of TDS or TCS already suffered elsewhere, and asks your employer to take them into account. Two rules limit what these declarations can do.

body.caption: What your employer can and cannot factor in

cells: Other income, such as FD interest or rent received
Increases estimated tax, so TDS goes up
TDS deducted by others, such as your bank, or TCS you paid
Reduces salary TDS, because that tax is already paid
Loss from a let-out or self-occupied house property (old regime)
Losses from shares, F&O or business
Cannot be used to reduce salary TDS

body.title: Scenario: Should Neha Tell Payroll About Her FDs?
body.scenario: Neha, an architect in Kolkata, earns ₹18,00,000 in the new regime. She also expects ₹80,000 of FD interest this year, on which her bank will deduct ₹8,000 as TDS. Her employer currently deducts ₹1,50,800 a year based on salary alone.
body.prompt: What happens at the end of the year if she says nothing, and what changes if she declares both the interest and the bank TDS to her employer?
body.modelAnswer: Her true tax on ₹18,80,000 of income is ₹1,67,440 (taxable ₹18,05,000, slab tax ₹1,61,000, plus 4% cess). If she says nothing, total TDS is ₹1,50,800 from salary plus ₹8,000 from the bank = ₹1,58,800. She would owe ₹8,640 when filing her return. If she declares both, payroll adds the interest to her estimate and credits the ₹8,000 already deducted, so salary TDS becomes ₹1,59,440 for the year. Total TDS then matches her tax, and there is no bill at filing time. Here the shortfall is small, but with larger interest, rent or capital gains it can cross the ₹10,000 advance tax threshold and start attracting interest, so declaring is usually the cleaner option.

children.text: Check Your Own Payslip

body.title: Try It: Estimate Monthly TDS
body.prompt: Sunil, a sales manager in Indore, earns a salary of ₹16,00,000 in tax year 2026-27, stays in the new regime and has no other income or declarations. What should his monthly TDS be?
body.explanation: Taxable income is ₹16,00,000 minus ₹75,000 = ₹15,25,000. Slab tax: ₹20,000 (5% on 4L to 8L) plus ₹40,000 (10% on 8L to 12L) plus ₹48,750 (15% on ₹3,25,000) = ₹1,08,750. Add 4% cess of ₹4,350 for ₹1,13,100. Spread over 12 months, that is ₹9,425 a month.

body.title: Recompute Your Own Salary TDS
steps: From your payslip or offer letter, note your projected gross salary for tax year 2026-27
Confirm with HR which regime payroll is using for you
Subtract the standard deduction and, in the old regime, your declared exemptions and deductions
Apply the slab rates from this lesson, then any rebate or marginal relief, then add 4% cess
Divide by 12 and compare with the income tax line on your payslip. If it is off by more than a few hundred rupees, ask payroll for its tax computation sheet

cards.definition: TDS on salary under the Income-tax Act, 2025, at the average rate on estimated annual income. Formerly Section 192.
Estimated annual tax divided by estimated taxable income. Salary TDS is spread using this rate, not the top slab rate.
Standard deduction for salaried employees: ₹75,000 in the new regime and ₹50,000 in the old. Formerly Section 16.
Rebate that removes tax on taxable income up to ₹12,00,000 in the new regime (₹5,00,000 in the old). Formerly Section 87A.
Caps new-regime tax at the amount by which taxable income exceeds ₹12,00,000, so crossing the limit slightly does not create a large bill.
The new tax regime, which is the default for salary TDS unless you opt out. Formerly Section 115BAC.
Employee's declaration of deductions, exemptions and proofs to the employer for salary TDS. Formerly Form 12BB.

points: Salary TDS under Section 392 is based on your estimated tax for the whole year, not on each month in isolation
Every month, payroll deducts (estimated annual tax minus TDS so far) divided by the months remaining, so mid-year changes hit the later months harder
Slabs for tax year 2026-27 are unchanged. In the new regime, a salary up to ₹12,75,000 attracts no TDS because of the standard deduction and the Section 156 rebate
Marginal relief caps new-regime tax just above ₹12,00,000 of taxable income at the excess over that limit, plus cess
The new regime is the default. Tell your employer at the start of the year if you want the old regime and submit proofs through Form 124
Declaring other income and TDS deducted elsewhere to payroll avoids a surprise tax bill when you file your return

Rates, rebates and provisions reflect the position understood at the time of writing and can change with each Union Budget.
